title: test-0133-SOC-GEO-DRAINAGE
passage: The drainage system of India is shaped by the diverse relief features of the subcontinent. Himalayan rivers, such as the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra, are perennial because they are fed by both melting snow from glaciers and seasonal rainfall. These rivers traverse vast areas, creating extensive drainage basins that include the main river and all its tributaries, covering thousands of square kilometers. In contrast, Peninsular rivers like the Narmada and Tapti flow westwards into the Arabian Sea, defying the common assumption that all Indian rivers flow towards the Bay of Bengal. The health of these river systems is currently under threat. While industrial effluents are a major concern, the excessive use of chemical fertilizers in agriculture and the discharge of untreated domestic sewage are equally responsible for the rising levels of river pollution. Monitoring these water bodies is essential, as the total catchment area of the Ganga basin alone spans over 860,000 square kilometers, supporting millions of people. Understanding these patterns helps us manage our water resources more effectively, ensuring that both the perennial northern rivers and the seasonal southern rivers remain sustainable for future generations.
summary: These rivers traverse vast areas, creating extensive drainage basins that include the main river and all its tributaries, covering thousands of square kilometers. Understanding these patterns helps us manage our water resources more effectively, so both the northern rivers and southern rivers can keep their water for future generations.
